title: Knowledge Organisers
content_html:
Structured notes

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic — the whole picture at a glance.

What the Research Says

A knowledge organiser is a single side of A4 that captures everything a student needs to know about a topic — key vocabulary, essential facts, core concepts, and connections between them. Used properly, it becomes the base layer of your revision: the thing you keep coming back to, the thing you redraw from memory, the thing you carry on the bus. Used badly, it becomes a wall of dense text that nobody reads.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Willingham (2017)Students need to store facts in long-term memory before they can think critically about them. Knowledge organisers are the storage scaffold.Not old-fashioned — cognitive prerequisite for analysis.
Counsell (2018)Used in UK schools to reduce cognitive load by pre-structuring the material students encounter.Reduces working memory demand during lessons.
Sweller (1988)Cognitive Load Theory: well-organised schemas free up working memory for higher-order tasks.A well-designed organiser makes hard questions easier.
Oakes & Griffin (2017)Students who made their OWN organisers outperformed those given finished ones.Making is learning. Receiving is not.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    One topic per organiser — a unit, a theme, a mythological cycle. Not the whole of Myth & Religion. Too broad and it becomes a dense textbook page.
  2. 2
    Divide the page into 4–6 sections — typically: Key Vocabulary, Key Sources (literary and material), Core Concepts, Sketch Visuals, Connections to Other Topics, Common Exam Questions. The structure forces you to categorise.
  3. 3
    Keep it to one side of A4 — the constraint is the point. If it doesn’t fit, the material isn’t yet compressed into the essentials.
  4. 4
    Use tiny structural visuals — a mini temple plan showing the naos and pronaos, a compact sketch of the Lion Gate, a small table of the three orders. Dual coding applies: words + visuals beat words alone.
  5. 5
    Redraw it from memory weekly — this is where the learning is. A finished organiser you never revisit is wasted. The redrawn one is retrieval practice in disguise.
  6. 6
    Annotate over time — when you learn something new that fits, add it. When a connection becomes clearer, draw the link. The organiser evolves.
Example 1

Create a knowledge organiser for the Olympian gods. Sections: Key Vocabulary (deity, attribute, epithet, cult, festival); a table of all twelve Olympians with their domain, principal symbol, and Roman equivalent (Zeus / Jupiter, Hera / Juno, Poseidon / Neptune, Demeter / Ceres, Athena / Minerva, Apollo / Apollo, Artemis / Diana, Ares / Mars, Aphrodite / Venus, Hephaestus / Vulcan, Hermes / Mercury, Dionysus / Bacchus); a mini sketch of one deity’s attributes; Key Myths (one per deity, maximum five words); Connections (links to temple architecture — which deities had the most important cult temples and why). Fit it on one side of A4, redraw from memory after three days. The Roman equivalents column is the most commonly dropped under exam pressure.

Example 2

Create a knowledge organiser for the material culture of Mycenae. Sections: Key Vocabulary (citadel, megaron, cyclopean, shaft grave, tholos tomb, fresco); Key Sites and Artefacts (Lion Gate — function + heraldic lions; Grave Circle A — shaft graves, gold masks, evidence of elite burial; Treasury of Atreus — tholos form, corbelled entrance, Bronze Age engineering; the megaron — central hearth, throne, four columns, fresco programme); a tiny annotated sketch of the citadel layout; Connections to the Odyssey (feasting in the great hall, the palace of Alcinous, descriptions of bronze and gold wealth). Redraw the sketch from memory a week later — the relative positions of the Lion Gate, Grave Circle A, and the megaron are the most frequently mixed up, and source questions reward students who can place artefacts in their architectural context.

Common Pitfalls

  • Copying the textbook. A dense page of 8pt text isn’t a knowledge organiser — it’s a photocopy. Compress ruthlessly.
  • One page per subject. Too much, too diffuse. One page per topic — one for the Olympians, one for temple architecture, one for Mycenae, one for the Odyssey episodes.
  • Making one and never revisiting. The value is in the redrawing — not the original creation.
  • Using a downloaded one instead of making your own. Research is clear: making beats receiving. Teacher-provided organisers are useful for structure only.

When to Use This

Start one at the beginning of each topic, as you’re learning it. Refine as your understanding grows. Redraw the whole set from memory in the final month before exams — one topic per day. Carry a folder of your organisers to every revision session. Use them as the spine of retrieval practice: cover the organiser, brain-dump, then check.

Quick Reference
~45 minutes to create, 15 to redraw
